summary:
SOLARIS (A Space Dream) : An Interactive 3D Space Mission Design Game

SOLARIS is an interactive 3D game that allows players to experience the journey of designing, building, launching, and operating a space mission. Inspired by the excitement surrounding India's Chandrayaan missions, we wanted to make space exploration something people could experience rather than just watch.

Players take on the role of astronaut-engineers, collect spacecraft components, assemble satellites, and manage missions in orbit while balancing real-world constraints such as mass, power, budget, and communication. Through interactive mini-games, mission simulations, quizzes, and explainable feedback, players learn why engineering decisions lead to success or failure and can improve their designs through repeated attempts.

SOLARIS addresses the challenge by turning complex space mission design concepts into an engaging, practical learning experience. Its collaborative gameplay, competency-based learning, and leaderboard encourage teamwork and healthy competition.

Our goal is to make space science accessible to everyone, inspire curiosity about the universe, and encourage the next generation to explore aerospace, astronomy, and space technology.
details:
SOLARIS: A Space Dream

An Interactive 3D Space Mission Design and Simulation Game

1. The Inspiration Behind SOLARIS

Growing up in India, most of us have heard the names of Rakesh Sharma and Kalpana Chawla. Their journeys made space exploration something we could dream about, even if we had never imagined becoming astronauts ourselves. We read about planets, rockets and astronauts in textbooks, watched documentaries and wondered what existed beyond our planet. Yet, space exploration often remained something distant, technically complex and difficult to experience firsthand.

In 2019, millions of Indians watched as Chandrayaan-2's Vikram lander approached the lunar surface. During its final descent, communication with the lander was lost approximately two kilometres above the Moon. Although the landing did not go as planned, the mission demonstrated the immense challenges involved in space exploration.

When Chandrayaan-3 began its journey, something remarkable happened. People across the country followed almost every update. Students, families, children and people from different backgrounds eagerly awaited the landing. They explored lunar images, followed mission updates and became increasingly curious about what was happening millions of kilometres away.

We realised that people were not simply watching a space mission; they wanted to understand it. They wanted to know how spacecraft worked, how they reached the Moon and what happened behind the scenes.

This made us ask an important question:

What if people could do more than watch a space mission? What if they could actually experience what it takes to make one happen?

That question became the inspiration behind SOLARIS – A Space Dream.

2. The Problem We Identified

Space exploration is fascinating, but understanding how real missions are designed and operated can be challenging for beginners.

A space mission is not simply about building a rocket and sending it into space. It involves interconnected spacecraft systems, engineering decisions, scientific objectives, resource limitations and continuous coordination.

For example, designing even a small CubeSat requires decisions about its structure, scientific instruments, power generation, battery capacity, communication systems, orientation, launch compatibility and mission lifetime.

Every component affects the others.

  • A more powerful scientific instrument may improve observations but increase mass, power consumption and cost.
  • A larger battery may help a satellite survive an eclipse but also add weight and expense.
  • A high-capacity communication system may transmit more data but require additional power and equipment.

These are real engineering trade-offs, where there is rarely one perfect solution.

However, beginners often encounter these concepts through textbooks, videos and isolated educational activities. They may learn what a satellite is or how an orbit works, but rarely get the opportunity to understand how all these systems work together.

Another challenge is accessibility. Many technical simulation tools are designed for people with scientific or engineering backgrounds, making their terminology, calculations and interfaces intimidating for beginners.

At the same time, much of today's digital engagement revolves around short-form content and endless scrolling, leaving an opportunity to make screen time more meaningful and intellectually engaging.

The problem we aim to solve is the gap between curiosity and experience: How can we make complex space exploration accessible while transforming passive screen time into active learning, experimentation and discovery?

3. Our Solution: SOLARIS

SOLARIS is an interactive 3D space mission design and simulation game that allows players to experience the complete journey of a space mission, from planning and spacecraft assembly to launch and orbital operations.

Players take on the role of astronaut-engineers working at a launch site. Instead of simply reading about spacecraft components, they explore their environment, collect parts, assemble satellites, launch them and manage their missions in space.

The central idea is to teach engineering through experience.

Every component offers advantages and limitations. Every decision influences the mission. Players must understand the consequences of their choices, manage limited resources and find solutions to unexpected challenges.

SOLARIS is built around one principle:

Learn by doing. Understand by experimenting. Improve by failing and trying again.

4. How Does SOLARIS Work?

The gameplay follows a connected space mission journey.

A. Mission Briefing

Every mission begins with a specific objective and a set of engineering requirements.

For example, players may receive a challenge to design a CubeSat to monitor crop health across India, within a budget of $380,000 and a mass limit of 4 kg.

The briefing establishes requirements involving the spacecraft frame, scientific payload, power, communications, pointing accuracy, budget and other constraints.

Players must understand the mission objectives before making design decisions.

B. Collecting Components and Building the Satellite

Players explore seven colour-coded zones, each representing a major spacecraft subsystem:

  1. Frame and Structure
  2. Solar Panels
  3. Battery
  4. Onboard Computer
  5. Radio and Communication
  6. Pointing and Attitude Control
  7. Scientific Payload

Players collect components and assemble their satellite at the launch pad.

The interface displays live resource indicators, including spacecraft mass, total cost, solar power generation, power consumption and battery requirements.

This helps players understand how individual components contribute to the overall mission.

C. Engineering Trade-offs

This is one of the most important learning elements of SOLARIS.

Every component offers benefits but introduces additional constraints.

For example:

  • A better camera can improve scientific observations but increase mass, power consumption and data generation.
  • A larger battery can provide more energy during an eclipse but increase spacecraft weight and cost.
  • A more capable radio can improve communication but may require additional power.

Players must balance competing requirements instead of simply selecting the most expensive or powerful components.

There can be multiple successful spacecraft designs. The game evaluates how effectively players manage resources and satisfy mission requirements.

D. Launch and Orbit

Once the satellite is assembled, players move to the launch stage.

The spacecraft must satisfy launch requirements. If it exceeds the permitted mass, it may fail to lift. Players also experience skill-based ascent controls that influence the fuel remaining after launch.

After a successful launch, players observe their satellite orbiting Earth.

The orbital environment introduces additional challenges. When a spacecraft passes through Earth's shadow, its solar panels cannot generate power. If its battery capacity is insufficient, the satellite may lose power.

This demonstrates the relationship between orbital conditions, solar energy, battery sizing and mission lifetime.

E. Mission Operations: Four Interactive Mini-Games

SOLARIS includes four short, replayable operational challenges that introduce important concepts in spacecraft operations.

1. Downlink Rush

Players assign ground-station antennas to satellite communication passes to ensure that valuable scientific data is transmitted before communication windows close.

Concepts: Communication windows, ground stations and data transmission.

2. Eclipse Energy

Players schedule scientific instruments and heaters while managing battery capacity during periods without sunlight.

Concepts: Energy management, battery capacity and eclipse operations.

3. Mission Sequencer

Players arrange command blocks to plan spacecraft activities for an orbit and identify errors in their mission sequence.

Concepts: Mission planning, scheduling and operational logic.

4. Orbit Burn

Players plan orbital manoeuvres to reach a target orbit while working with limited fuel.

Concepts: Orbital mechanics, manoeuvres and delta-v.

These mini-games transform technical concepts into practical challenges that players can understand through interaction.

One of the playable mission-selection screens in SOLARIS, showcasing its interactive game interface, mission options, flight modes, and hands-on space exploration experience.

F. Mission Control Live

Real space missions do not always go according to plan.

SOLARIS introduces unexpected situations such as:

  • Solar flares
  • Reaction-wheel failures
  • Ground-station outages
  • Budget cuts

Players must respond to these events and make decisions under pressure.

This introduces the importance of risk management, redundancy, reliability and operational decision-making.

G. Results, Feedback and Improvement

At the end of a mission, players receive a score ranging from zero to three stars, along with an explanation of their performance.

Instead of simply displaying whether a mission succeeded or failed, SOLARIS provides numerical feedback explaining the reasons behind the outcome.

For example, a player may discover that their spacecraft required approximately 16 Wh of battery capacity to survive an eclipse but had only 10 Wh available.

Players can compare their designs with relevant real-world missions, understand their mistakes and use the fix-and-retry approach to improve their next attempt.

System Architecture & Workflow diagram illustrating how SOLARIS integrates interactive gameplay, satellite components, mission operations, and learning assessment into a unified space mission simulation.

5. Learning Through Experience

Our objective is not to make players memorise aerospace terminology. We want them to understand concepts precisely when those concepts become relevant.

For example:

  • Selecting a battery introduces energy capacity.
  • Entering Earth's shadow demonstrates why battery storage matters.
  • Transmitting scientific data introduces communication windows and downlink limitations.
  • Planning an orbital manoeuvre introduces delta-v and fuel requirements.

SOLARIS also provides contextual hints, short explanations and a glossary covering technical terms such as eclipse, delta-v, link budget and depth of discharge.

The game offers two difficulty modes:

Explorer Mode: Provides hints and more generous resource margins for beginners.

Mission Director Mode: Introduces tighter constraints and unexpected events for players seeking advanced challenges.

This approach makes space science approachable without removing the engineering challenges that make mission design interesting.

6. Collaboration and Teamwork

Real space missions are developed by multidisciplinary teams. SOLARIS brings this collaborative experience into gameplay.

The concept supports collaborative missions for up to four players, with specialised responsibilities:

  • Mission Planner: Defines objectives and manages mission requirements.
  • Spacecraft Engineer: Handles spacecraft components and engineering constraints.
  • Science Lead: Focuses on scientific objectives and payload selection.
  • Operations and Communications Lead: Manages mission operations and data transmission.

Each role brings a different perspective.

For example, the Science Lead may want a more powerful instrument, while the Spacecraft Engineer must consider whether its additional mass exceeds the mission limit.

Players must communicate, negotiate and make decisions while working with a shared spacecraft and budget.

This demonstrates that successful space missions depend on collaboration as much as technical knowledge.

SOLARIS features four interactive game modes—Tesseract: Mission Design, Daily Learning Quiz, Signal Run, and Deep Space Lab—each designed to make space science engaging through hands-on challenges, gameplay, and practical learning.

7. Innovation and What Makes SOLARIS Different

The key innovation of SOLARIS lies in combining space science, interactive gaming and experiential learning within one connected experience.

Unlike traditional educational resources that primarily explain individual concepts, SOLARIS allows players to understand how spacecraft systems interact and how engineering decisions affect an entire mission.

Our major differentiators include:

  1. Interactive 3D Space Environment: Explore and experience a simulated space mission rather than passively consuming information.
  2. Hands-on Satellite Assembly: Collect components and construct spacecraft using different subsystems.
  3. Real Engineering Trade-offs: Balance mass, power, battery, communication, data and budget.
  4. Mission-Based Mini-Games: Learn spacecraft operations through practical challenges.
  5. Explainable Feedback: Understand why a mission succeeds or fails through numerical explanations.
  6. Learning Through Failure: Experiment, redesign and improve without treating failure as the end of the learning process.
  7. Competency-Based Learning: Reinforce understanding through quizzes, progress tracking and leaderboards.
  8. Collaborative Gameplay: Introduce multidisciplinary roles and shared decision-making.
  9. Adaptive Difficulty: Make the experience approachable for beginners while retaining challenges for advanced players.

Our goal is not to create another complicated aerospace simulator. It is to make the engineering behind space exploration understandable and enjoyable for people without a technical background.

End-to-end SOLARIS gameplay workflow, illustrating the complete player journey from mission briefing and satellite assembly to validation, rocket launch, orbital operations, performance assessment, and continuous improvement through retry-based learning.

8. NASA Research and Resources

During the development of SOLARIS, we explored NASA's mission development frameworks and educational resources to understand how real spacecraft missions are planned, designed and operated.

Our research references include:

  • NASA General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT)
  • NASA Mission Design Lab
  • Concept Maturity Levels
  • NASA Mission Viz
  • NASA CubeSat 101 Handbook

These resources informed our understanding of mission objectives, spacecraft subsystems, engineering requirements, mission analysis and design trade-offs.

We also considered the four major mission segments: launch, space, ground and user. This helped us approach space exploration as a complete mission lifecycle rather than focusing only on the spacecraft.

9. Technology Stack and Development Considerations

SOLARIS combines programming, 3D modelling and scientific computing to create an interactive simulation-based learning experience.

Technology Stack:

  • Primary Programming Language: Python
  • 3D Game Engine: Panda3D / Ursina
  • 3D Modelling and Animation: Blender
  • Scientific Computing: NumPy, SciPy
  • Interactive 3D Visualisation: VPython
  • Version Control: Git and GitHub
  • Mission Design Research: NASA GMAT and Mission Design Lab

During development, we considered both the technical requirements of spacecraft simulation and the overall player experience.

Major engineering considerations include:

  1. Spacecraft mass and structural limitations.
  2. Power generation and battery capacity.
  3. Payload selection and component costs.
  4. Data generation and communication windows.
  5. Launch compatibility and orbital conditions.
  6. Fuel requirements and mission lifetime.

We also prioritised beginner-friendly explanations, interface simplicity, accessibility, replayability, performance and collaboration.

Our objective was to balance educational accuracy with engaging gameplay so players could explore complex ideas without feeling overwhelmed.

10. Intended Impact and Our Vision

SOLARIS aims to make space exploration more accessible by turning scientific curiosity into an interactive experience.

For children and young learners: It offers an opportunity to explore science beyond textbooks and discover an interest in space.

For school and college students: It introduces practical engineering concepts through simulations, experimentation and decision-making.

For educators and institutions: It offers a supplementary platform for making STEM education more interactive.

For space enthusiasts and the general public: It makes spacecraft design and mission operations approachable without requiring an engineering background.

Beyond education, SOLARIS encourages a shift in how people use digital technology. Instead of limiting screen time to passive entertainment, we want to make it an opportunity for creativity, exploration, critical thinking and discovery.

We hope to inspire young people to explore opportunities in aerospace, astronomy, scientific research, gaming and technology.

Perhaps someone who plays SOLARIS today will become tomorrow's space scientist, aerospace engineer, researcher, game developer or astronaut.

We grew up inspired by pioneers like Rakesh Sharma and Kalpana Chawla. We witnessed how Chandrayaan-3 brought millions of people together through curiosity and excitement.

Through SOLARIS, we want to bring that feeling closer to everyone.

Our vision is to turn spectators into explorers, consumers into creators, curiosity into knowledge and the dream of space exploration into an experience accessible to all.

Explore our GitHub repository to discover the project architecture, source code, development resources and implementation details of SOLARIS.

We have documented our development journey, technical approach and key project components to make our work transparent and accessible.

Check out SOLARIS, explore the code, and follow our journey: Solaris :- A Space Dream

FROM SCREEN TIME TO SPACE TIME.

LESS SCROLLING, MORE EXPLORING.

We don't just learn about the future; we learn by Building it.
